title: 50 Years of Chickens: 9 Mistakes That Cost Me 40 Hens
description:
Fifty years of keeping hens, and I wrote down every one I lost. These are the nine mistakes that cost me the most: forty hens in all, what happened, the first sign I missed, what fixed it, and what the fix cost. The biggest one wasn't a fox or a raccoon. It was bringing new birds straight home to my flock.

The nine:
9. The wrong roost: high, skinny perches → bumblefoot. Fix: a 2x4, wide side up, 2-3 ft high, 8-10 inches per hen (~$5).
8. Too many treats: scraps and treats no more than about 10% of what they eat. Never moldy food, avocado skin or pit, raw dry beans, or salty food.
7. No oyster shell: crushed oyster shell in its OWN dish, free choice (~$8 for 5 lb). Know the difference between a broody hen and an egg-bound hen.
6. Too many roosters: about one rooster per ten hens. Hens don't need a rooster to lay.
5. A wet coop: waterer outside, up on blocks; shovel out wet spots the same day. Coccidiosis is treated with amprolium in the water.
4. A coop shut up too tight: frostbite comes from moisture, not cold. Vents up high, no draft across the roost (rule of thumb: ~1 sq ft of vent per 10 sq ft of floor).
3. Chicken wire: it keeps chickens in, not predators out. 1/2" hardware cloth, screwed down with washers, plus a wire apron.
2. The heat lamp: a fire risk in dry bedding, and grown hens don't need it. For chicks, a flat heating plate.
1. No quarantine: every new bird gets at least 30 days apart, cared for last, checked every day.

This is a personal account from one small Indiana flock, not veterinary advice. If a bird is sick, call your vet or your county extension office.
